content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to tackle the problem of  Heterogeneous Continual Learning, a continual learning setting without any restriction on the representation's training configuration or network architecture. 
The authors also provide a solution to solve this problem: 
(1) Using knowledge distillation, where the last step model(a weak model) is the teacher model while the current model (a stronger model) is the student model.
(2)  Using a modified version of DeepInversion(DI), which removes the dependency on the previous data. 
The experiments report significant improvements in various benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+  This paper is clearly written, and the experimental results are quite strong. 
+  It is a good idea to remove the dependencies on the previous data by using DeepInversion(DI).
 
Weakness:
- This paper claim that "To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that explores continual learning with different representational structures while adapting to the current task and minimizing catastrophic forgetting." But this is not true. Continual learning with changing architectures have been studied in previous work[a][b][c]. Besides, as continual learning approaches, they all try to tackle the "catastrophic forgetting" problem.

[a] R. Istrate, A. C. I. Malossi, C. Bekas, D. Nikolopoulos, Incremental training of deep convolutional neural networks, arXiv preprint arXiv:1803.10232.

[b] S. S. Sarwar, A. Ankit, K. Roy, Incremental learning in deep convolutional neural networks using partial network sharing, arXiv preprint arXiv:1712.02719.

[c] Jaehong Yoon, Eunho Yang, Jeongtae Lee, Sung Ju Hwang. Lifelong learning with dynamically expandable networks.

- The novelty is limited. It can be seen in Table 2: The most effective part of the method is KD, while the main difference from the previous method is image augmentation.   The novelty of the Quick Deep Inversion is minor, which modifies the start point. Equation 4  is not CLEAR to me. The step $k$ didn't appear in the loss terms.

- The results are strange. For example, in Table 1, the proposed method only using KD is much better than the previous methods. Even without data augmentation and label smoothing, the performance is much better than LwF, which is also a KD-based method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty is limited.
As I have described in the weakness:
(1) The setting is not new. Previous methods have considered continual learning with changing architecture. 
(2) The method is incremental: the existing KD method with label smooth and data augmentation and modification of DI.
content.summary_of_the_review: I lean to reject this paper for three reasons: (1) The core setting is not new, but the authors think it is. (2) The method is not novel. (3) The results are not persuasive.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response to Reviewer tLHp
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,

Thank you for your review and your thoughtful comments. We appreciate you finding our paper clearly written with strong experimental results. We clarify the differences with architectural methods in the common response. Further, we respond to your other concerns below:

> The novelty is limited. It can be seen in Table 2: The most effective part of the method is KD, while the main difference from the previous method is image augmentation. The novelty of the Quick Deep Inversion is minor, which modifies the start point. 

We respectfully disagree that the novelty of our method is limited:
* First, we emphasize that our work makes the first attempt to conduct continual learning on the new tasks with changing network architecture without any constraints on the number of layers, network design, and so on. To this end, our proposed benchmarks are composed of ten different architectures proposed in the past decade.
* Second, we show that the adaption of advances in knowledge distillation can outperform state-of-the-art continual learning methods, which should provide insights for the development of future CL techniques.
* Third, we propose QDI, which shows a significant speedup for data-free CL methods with better/comparable performance across all benchmarks.

---

> The results are strange. For example, in Table 1, the proposed method only using KD is much better than the previous methods. Even without data augmentation and label smoothing, the performance is much better than LwF, which is also a KD-based method.

LwF uses fixed teacher (pre-computed logits) for knowledge distillation. On the contrary, we compute the logits using the same views/images for both the teacher and student during training, which has also shown significant improvement in knowledge distillation in prior works [1].

---

We thank you again for your time and efforts in reviewing our paper, as well as for the constructive comments and suggestions.

Thank you,    
Authors.   

---

### References
[1] Beyer et al. Knowledge distillation: A good teacher is patient and consistent. CVPR 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper defines and studies Heterogeneous Continual Learning (HCL), where a wide range of evolving architectures are trained continually. The proposed method includes several components and tricks to tackle this problem. First, knowledge distillation with low temperature is used. Second, the authors use data augmentation. Finally, the proposed method uses Quick Deep Inversion (QDI), which is an extension of DeepInversion (DI) for data efficiency. The authors show the effectiveness of the proposed method through extensive experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths


- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.


- The proposed method shows strong performance. In addition, not needing task identifiers and replay data is a major advantage.



### weaknesses


- The major weakness of the paper is that it does not provide many additional insights into the community. While the empirical results seem strong, I do not find enough explanation behind *why* would different decisions and components be beneficial in terms of forward/backward transfer. For instance, at a very high level, why would changing architecture be beneficial for reducing forgetting? How does label smoothing impact forward/backward transfer in Table 5? Overall, I believe the lack of explanations and insights that can justify the results is the main weakness of the paper.


- As the authors mentioned in Sec. 5, the proposed method needs careful selection of hyper-parameters and requires additional hyper-parameters (e.g., A.1.2).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and well-organized, and experimental results support the claims. In terms of novelty, I find the paper mostly relies on recent advances in other fields (e.g., KD, DI, etc.). Finally, regarding reproducibility, the authors clearly explain their experimental setup and claim that they will release their code.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the proposed method relies on several other works, I find the results interesting. However, I believe the lack of explanation behind *why* and *how* each component of the proposed method contributes to forward/backward transfer (potentially with more controlled experiments), makes it a borderline paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer a1uo
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,

Thank you for your review and your thoughtful comments. We appreciate you finding our paper well-written, and easy to follow with strong performance. We respond to your concern regarding the lack of explanations and insights of our proposed method in the common response. Further, we respond to your other concerns below:

> Why would changing architecture be beneficial for reducing forgetting?

 We clarify that we do not claim that changing the architecture would be beneficial to reduce forgetting. Instead, updating the network architecture is helpful for the current and future task performance, as demonstrated in Figure 2. To this end, it allows the continual update of the state-of-the-art architecture instead of continuing training for architectures proposed many years ago, as also demonstrated in Figure 2 of our paper. Further, it is a comparatively more challenging task in comparison to the standard CL due to the reinitialization of network structures. 

---

> As the authors mentioned in Sec. 5, the proposed method needs careful selection of hyper-parameters and requires additional hyper-parameters (e.g., A.1.2).

We follow the same hyper-parameter setup (learning rate) as existing works [1] for training all the network architectures. Contrarily, different architectures might have different optimal hyper-parameter setup, which would be an interesting direction for future work. 

---

We thank you again for your time and efforts in reviewing our paper, as well as for the constructive comments and suggestions.

Thank you,       
Authors

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper firstly proposes a relaxation of the typical continual learning setup in which the architecture of the neural network is allowed to change over time. As a solution for this problem, the paper proposes a method which combines various different approaches: knowledge distillation, pseudo-replay using a modified version of deep inversion, data augmentation and label smoothing.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
There is a lot going on in this paper.

Let’s start with the new setting of “heterogeneous continual learning” that is proposed. I struggle to understand the rationale for this setting, it seems rather contrived to me. Is my understanding correct that the “use-case” of this setting is as follows: we have trained a particular neural network on a particular set of data, and then this data goes away. Later new data becomes available, as well as a new, more effective neural network architecture. As a solution for the above problem, the authors note that we should do knowledge distillation.
I’m afraid this setting seems very contrived to me, while the proposed solution of knowledge distillation seems a logical if not straight-forward solution for this problem.

The authors also propose a method that besides knowledge distillation also makes use of pseudo-replay using a modified version of deep inversion, data augmentation and label smoothing. The authors then show that this combined method outperforms other recent methods on benchmarks such as Split CIFAR10 and Split TinyImageNet, in both task and class incremental learning settings.
This seems to be quite an engineering achievement, but I’m afraid that the usefulness of this demonstration for the continual learning literature is very limited. As far as I can see there do not seem to be any new insights that arise from these experiments. All components of the proposed method (knowledge distillation, pseudo-replay using a modified version of deep inversion, data augmentation and label smoothing) are well known to be useful strategies for continual learning, and it seems the authors have managed an engineering feat by combining these strategies into one method that works well on the Split CIFAR10 and Split TinyImageNet. If the goal of continual learning was to get the highest possible score on these benchmarks perhaps this study would be valuable, but this is not the goal. These continual learning benchmarks are useful because they could give us insights into what strategies work well for continual learning.
Unfortunately I was not able to extract any new insights from this paper.
One reason that I struggle to extract insights from the provided empirical comparisons is that it seems to me the authors compare their proposed method to other methods that used different sets of constraints / assumptions (e.g., no use of augmentations).

Other issues:
- In the introduction it is claimed that a likely reason why the human brain can continuously learn from orthogonal experiences without mutual interference, is that the human brain is continuously changing. This is used as motivation for the proposed model. As support for this claim two references are given, but I do not see how these references support this claim.
- Figure 2 is unclear. The accuracy on the y-axis, is it the accuracy on task 1, the accuracy on task 2, the accuracy on the current task or the joint accuracy? After finishing training on task 2, could you show a comparison between the task 1 performance of ResNet18 and of the “ours” model?

Some missing references:
- Van de Ven & Tolias (2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.07734) for Task-IL and Class-IL
- Chaudhry et al (2018, https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.10112) for average forgetting measure
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Mostly see above. Generally, I think the writing of the paper is quite clear, but yet the paper is difficult to read because there is so much going on. As somewhat of a side note, I think the clarity of the paper is also reduced by an abundant use of “novel” / “for the first time” / etc.

I don't have specific concerns regarding reproducibility, although as code is not provided reviewers are not able to fully check this.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although this paper seems to be a neat engineering achievement, I believe its usefulness for the continual learning literature is rather limited as I do not think that this work provides substantial new insights, while the proposed “heterogeneous continual learning” setting appears to be rather contrived.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to continually evolve the structure of the network for continual learning. When a new task comes, a new stronger network is initialized for learning the new task, and the knowledge from previous tasks is transferred to the new network via knowledge distillation. To enhance the knowledge distillation, pseudo data of the previous tasks recovered by a quick deep inversion mechanism is also adopted. Experiments are conducted on multiple datasets with different baselines, and the results are promising
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

* The idea to keep evolving the network for new tasks is good and can involve more flexibility than the existing knowledge distillation-based works with fixed network structures.

* The paper has a clear logic and is easy to follow.

* The experiment results are promising.

Weakness and questions:

1. The idea to evolve the network is not entirely new but resembles the parameter isolation-based methods like Dynamically Expandable Networks [1], which also keep changing the structure to accommodate new tasks.

2. When a new task comes, how is the new network initialized, and how is the structure decided? It is natural to expect the new structure can consider the information of new tasks, which is considered in Dynamically Expandable Networks. 

3. The QDI is not always improving the results, and the improvement is not obvious mostly. Sometimes it can even significantly degrade the performance (Table 2)  Since it requires extra computational resources, this module seems not beneficial and sometimes even detrimental.

4. The formulation of total variation and L_{l_2} is not given. And their motivations are not clear either. If L_{l_2} is simply l2 normalization, it seems also to restrict the variation.

5. The average forgetting is different from the ones used in existing works (e.g. the backward transfer in GEM [2]). Why is this?

6. Why are some results unavailable?

7. Although the idea resembles some parameter isolation based methods, no parameter isolation based methods are compared as baselines.

[1] Yoon, Jaehong, et al. "Lifelong learning with dynamically expandable networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1708.01547 (2017).
[2] Lopez-Paz, David, and Marc'Aurelio Ranzato. "Gradient episodic memory for continual learning." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has a certain novelty and satisfying clarity. But the quality and reproducibility are questionable due to the unclear parts mentioned above.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of combining evolving networks and knowledge distillation is good and experimentally promising. However, since some key parts of the work are unclear as explained in the weakness part, the current version cannot be accepted.

content.title: Response to Reviewer TRjt
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,

Thank you for your review and your thoughtful comments. We appreciate you finding our paper well-written and easy to follow with promising experimental results. We have addressed your concerns regarding the comparison with expansion methods in our common response. Further, we clarify your concerns regarding computational constraints and comparison with class-incremental baselines below.

> When a new task comes, how is the new network initialized, and how is the structure decided? It is natural to expect the new structure can consider the information of new tasks, which is considered in Dynamically Expandable Networks.

The new network is randomly initialized when the architecture of the current task is different from the previous task. To replicate real-world scenarios, the structure of the architectures is decided based on the deep-learning advances on the ImageNet challenge over the past decade.

---

> The QDI is not always improving the results, and the improvement is not obvious mostly. Sometimes it can even significantly degrade the performance (Table 2) Since it requires extra computational resources, this module seems not beneficial and sometimes even detrimental.

We want to emphasize that QDI improves the performance across all the settings except the Class-IL setting for the Split CIFAR-10 dataset, and we firmly believe this module is beneficial. We have already clarified this exception in the class-incremental continual learning experimental evaluation paragraph.

---

> The formulation of total variation and L_{l_2} is not given. And their motivations are not clear either. If L_{l_2} is simply l2 normalization, it seems also to restrict the variation.

We adopt the total validation and $L_{\ell_2}$ from prior works [1,2], where they have been used as image priors. Further, we will add the formulation in the updated version.

---
> The average forgetting is different from the ones used in existing works (e.g. the backward transfer in GEM [2]). Why is this?

Following all the recent works [3,4,5,6], we report forgetting instead of backward transfer (as reported in GEM) .

---

> Why are some results unavailable?

We took the numbers for LwF, SI, iCARL from the DER [5] paper to fairly represent the distribution in our work. Unfortunately, the missing numbers were not reported in their paper.

---

We thank you again for your time and efforts in reviewing our paper, as well as for the constructive comments and suggestions.

Thank you,     
Authors

display_title: Response to all reviewers - Part I

content.title: Response to all reviewers - Part I
content.comment:
Dear all reviewers, 

Thank you for your review and your thoughtful comments. We clarify the common concerns raised by the reviewers below.

* **Motivation for the proposed setting:** Our proposed Heterogeneous Continual Learning is a *realistic scenario* essential for many practical applications. Prior CL works have been continually adapting a *ResNet18* architecture, where all the methods train the same architecture from scratch for all the tasks. However, this setting is impractical in real-world applications, where we must deploy and continually update the state-of-the-art deep-learning architectures and techniques instead of continually updating the architecture proposed many years ago. Our work is the first step in this direction, where we can transfer the learned knowledge from any architecture to a new one and then continually learn the new architectural structure/representations. We provide various examples to illustrate the utility of the proposed framework below:
   * **Clinical diagnosis:** Consider the scenario of ResNet deployed in the hospital for disease diagnosis. The hospital continues to collect data with time and continually updates the ResNet architecture. Meanwhile, recent architectures such as RegNet outperform ResNet on the current task distribution. However, current CL methods do not support the knowledge transfer to a new architecture and require the training of RegNet on the complete data distribution, which is contrary to learning continual representations. 
   * **Autonomous vehicles:** Consider another scenario of U-Net for segmentation in self-driving cars. With the change in demographics, driving conditions, and distribution shifts, it is necessary to incorporate state-of-the-art advances and update the model structure to improve the current task accuracy.

Additionally, our setting is applicable and observed in various applications, including speech recognition, language modeling, and so on, where the architectures have progressed from RNNs to CNNs to transformer-based architectures.

We motivate these examples in Figure 2, where we show the benefit of adapting to novel neural architectures for two tasks by comparing the standard buffer-based CL method (DER) and our proposed method. The traditional CL techniques continually update the same network architecture (LeNet) and obtain lower average/joint accuracy when trained on the second task due to catastrophic forgetting.
On the contrary, HCL allows the update to a new architecture structure (ResNet18) while preserving the past task knowledge trained with LeNet.

Further, our proposed training scheme is especially beneficial when past-task data is unavailable due to privacy concerns. It allows the adaptation to the new network structure for the new task by utilizing the saved model checkpoints. It enables training with different network structures without storing any past-task instances.

---

* **Comparison with expansion-based methods:** Our work is similar yet orthogonal to the expansion-based techniques in continual learning in various ways. We highlight the differences below:
    * First, the motivation and objective of both methods are different. Architectural methods aim to reduce forgetting without changing the underlying architecture. In contrast, our goal is not to reduce forgetting but to update the network structure to incorporate the recent advances in deep learning to improve the current task accuracy (see Figure 2). HCL is a comparatively more challenging task than the standard CL setting because the prior learned information is completely lost with the change in network structure.
    * Second, architectural methods expand the same architecture and then selectively adopt various techniques to sparsify the previous features. Contrarily, we do not extend the same architecture but introduce state-of-the-art architectures to the CL framework. HCL is essential because it allows the continual update of the SOTA architectures rather than continually updating outdated architectures.
     * Third, none of the prior expansion-based methods can be applied to HCL. Progressive neural networks instantiate a new column for the new task and require inputs from both columns; however, this cannot be utilized when the number of features, layers, and network structure is different between the two tasks. The same constraint limits DEN as it requires expansion across the same layer structures.

---
[we continue our response below]

content.title: Response to all reviewers - Part II
content.comment:
[see the previous comment for the first part of our response]

* **Justification for the choice of various components:** Despite the existence of multiple components, such as knowledge distillation, deep inversion, data augmentation, and label smoothing for CL, these methods have shown limited success for CL in comparison to replay-based methods. In this work, we focus on the HCL setting, a comparatively more challenging setting where the existing replay and regularization methods do not show impressive performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first attempt to combine them in a unified HCL framework that outperforms the state-of-the-art CL techniques. We justify our design for these components below:
  * **Knowledge distillation using data augmentation:** While KD has been used for many applications, recently, Beyer et al. [1] showed that fixed teachers do not work well and proposed various design choices that improved the performance by over 4% on the ImageNet benchmark. These simple improvements in the distillation paradigm allow knowledge distillation across a diverse range of network architectures and prevent the overfitting of the model on the current task data distribution, alleviating forgetting for heterogeneous continual learning.
  * **Label smoothing:** The motivation for using label smoothing was to produce better soft targets for KD, thereby improving the distillation performance and reducing the forgetting for HCL. However, there have been contradicting conclusions regarding the benefits of label smoothing for KD [2,3] and it has not been adopted for CL. Only recently, Chandrasegaran et al. [4] proposed the guidelines to adapt label smoothing for KD, which improves performance for standard CL and HCL, as demonstrated in Table 5.

Simplicity is the strength of our proposed method showing that knowledge distillation with pseudo replay can achieve significantly better performance than state-of-the-art regularisation or coreset selection methods. To this end, it improves the performance by up to 20-30% on average accuracy for CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet datasets for HCL. We hope our approach can provide valuable insights and pathways to design better HCL methods in the future.

---

Thank you,
Authors

### References
[1] Beyer et al. Knowledge distillation: A good teacher is patient and consistent. CVPR 2022.   
[2] Müller et al. When does label smoothing help? NeurIPS 2019.  
[3] Shen et al. Is label smoothing truly incompatible with knowledge distillation: An empirical study. ICLR 2021.  
[4] Chandrasegaran et al. Revisiting Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation Compatibility What was Missing? ICML 2022
